title: How NYC Open Mics Work: Sign-Ups, Costs & Times
excerpt: Bucket vs list sign-up, drink minimums, how early to arrive and what to expect at your first NYC open mic.
metaDescription: Bucket vs list sign-up, what a two item minimum means, how early to arrive and what NYC open mics cost. A practical guide for first-time comedians.
author: Adam Malev
body:
If you have never done an open mic in New York, the listings can be confusing. One says bucket. Another says list. A third says two item minimum, which sounds like a tax form. None of it explains what you actually do when you walk in the door.

Here is how comedy open mics in NYC work in practice.

## Bucket sign-up versus list sign-up

Almost every open mic uses one of two systems, and the difference decides when you should show up.

A bucket mic means everyone writes their name on a slip of paper and drops it in a bucket, hat or jar. The host draws names at random. Arriving early does not get you an earlier slot, it only guarantees you are in the draw before it closes. What matters is being there before the bucket is pulled.

A list mic is first come, first served. You write your name on a sheet and you go up in that order. Here arriving early matters a great deal. At popular list mics, comics turn up an hour before the posted start time to get a slot near the top, because the room empties out as the night goes on and the last few spots perform to almost nobody.

If a listing does not say which system a mic uses, assume list and arrive early. That mistake costs you nothing. The reverse mistake costs you the spot.

## What open mics in NYC cost

Of 417 comedy open mics listed on Comediq across New York, the Hudson Valley, Los Angeles and Austin, 128 are free. The most common price is five dollars. That is the honest answer to a question most beginners get wrong, because the advice circulating secondhand suggests New York is more expensive than it is.

The prices that look confusing are usually not prices at all. A one-drink minimum means you perform for free but have to buy one drink, which is a bar covering its costs for giving up a room on a slow night. A two-item minimum is the same idea with two purchases, usually at comedy clubs rather than bars, and it can mean food or drink. A few mics ask for a cash amount plus one item, which is a club charging for stage time and the bar charging separately.

Cash still matters. Plenty of NYC mics are cash only at the door, so bring small bills even when a listing shows a card-friendly venue.

## How early to arrive

For a list mic, thirty to sixty minutes before the posted start time is normal at busy rooms. For a bucket mic, arriving fifteen minutes early is usually enough, as long as you are there for the draw.

The posted time on any listing is the show time, not the sign-up time. Sign-up often opens an hour earlier and closes when the room is full. This single detail is the most common reason new comics show up and find they cannot get on.

## How long you get on stage

Most NYC open mics give between three and five minutes. Some bucket mics drop to two or three minutes when turnout is heavy, because the host has to fit everybody in. A handful of mics offer longer sets, usually seven minutes, and those tend to be harder to get into.

Set length is not fixed. It is decided by how many people show up that night. Prepare for the shorter end of the range, and you will never be the comic who gets the light early and has no ending ready.

## Do you need to be experienced?

No. Open mics exist specifically so that people can try material in front of a room. The audience at most NYC mics is other comedians waiting their turn, which is a tougher crowd than a real show but a far more forgiving one for a first attempt. Nobody there expects polish.

Some mics are explicitly [beginner-friendly](/beginner-friendly) and lower pressure than others. Those are worth starting with.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is bucket sign-up at an open mic?

Bucket sign-up means every comic writes their name on a slip and the host draws names at random to set the order. Arriving early does not improve your position, but you must be present before the draw closes.

### Do you have to pay to perform at open mics in NYC?

Not always. Of 417 mics listed on Comediq, 128 are [free](/free-mics). The most common price is five dollars, and many of the rest ask for a one-drink or two-item minimum rather than a cash fee.

### What does a two-item minimum mean at a comedy club?

It means you need to buy two items, usually food or drinks, to perform or attend. It is how the venue covers its costs rather than a charge for stage time.

### How early should you arrive at an NYC open mic?

For list mics, thirty to sixty minutes before the posted time. For bucket mics, around fifteen minutes before, provided you are there for the draw. The posted time is the show time, not the sign-up time.

### How long is a set at an NYC open mic?

Usually three to five minutes. It can drop to two or three minutes on busy nights, because the host adjusts set length to fit everyone who turns up.

### What night has the most open mics in New York?

[Wednesday](/open-mics/wednesday) is the busiest night across the city, though mics run every night of the week in all five boroughs.

## Find a mic

You can browse every [open mic currently running in New York](/open-mics) by night of the week or by borough, with the cost, sign-up method, and start time listed for each one.

Start with [Manhattan](/open-mics/manhattan), [Brooklyn](/open-mics/brooklyn) or [Queens](/open-mics/queens).

title: Open Mic Etiquette: What NYC Comics Wish You Knew
excerpt: Staying for other comics, respecting your time limit, handling the mic, and the mistakes that get you quietly remembered.
metaDescription: The unwritten rules of NYC comedy open mics: staying for other comics, respecting your time limit, handling the mic and what to do before your first set.
author: Adam Malev
body:
Nobody tells you the rules at an open mic because everyone assumes you already know them. You do not, and neither did they on their first night. Here is what experienced comics in New York expect from the room, and the mistakes that get you quietly remembered for the wrong reasons.

## Stay for other comics

This is the single biggest unwritten rule at comedy open mics, and breaking it is the fastest way to get a reputation.

If you perform and leave, you are treating the room as an audience for yourself while giving nothing back. At a typical NYC mic, the crowd is almost entirely other comedians, so everyone who walks out makes the room worse for whoever is next. Hosts notice. Other comics notice.

Stay for at least a few sets after yours. Stay for the whole thing when you can. Comics who stay get invited to things.

## Respect your time limit

Most NYC open mics give three to five minutes. When the host flashes the light, you have roughly thirty seconds to finish. Not thirty seconds to start a new bit.

Going over your time is not a sign of confidence. It takes time directly from the comics after you, and at a mic running thirty names deep, it can mean someone does not get up at all. Hosts remember who runs long. It is the most common reason a comic stops getting booked.

Time your set at home. Out loud, with a timer. It is always longer than you think.

## Handle the microphone properly

Take the mic out of the stand at the start and move the stand aside. Hand the mic back at the end. Do this once, smoothly, without a struggle.

Fumbling the mic stand for twenty seconds burns a chunk of a five-minute set and reads as unprepared. Practise it at home with a hairbrush if you have to. Nobody will know.

## Do not heckle, even as a joke

In a room full of comedians, the temptation to shout something funny is real. Resist it. You are not helping, and the person on stage is trying to work out whether a joke lands, which they cannot do if the room is reacting to you instead.

The same applies to loud talking at the back, scrolling with your screen brightness up, and laughing at your friend's table rather than the stage.

## Laugh honestly

You are not obliged to fake laughter, and experienced comics can tell when a laugh is polite. But sitting in stony silence at a mic because you are rehearsing your own set in your head is also a choice, and it makes the room harder for everyone.

Listen properly. Laugh when something is funny. That is the whole ask.

## Know the room before you book it

Mics differ. Some are brand new comics working out their first jokes. Some are working comics tightening material for paid spots. Some have a specific audience, such as women and nonbinary rooms or LGBTQ rooms, and turning up without knowing that is a bad look.

Check what kind of room it is before you sign up. Watching one before you perform at it is the best preparation there is. If you are starting out, the [beginner-friendly](/beginner-friendly) rooms are the easier place to begin.

## Pay what the room asks

Of 417 open mics listed on Comediq, 128 are [free](/free-mics). The rest ask for something, usually five dollars or a one-drink minimum. That is a venue covering its costs for giving up a room on a slow night.

Pay it without complaint, and bring cash because many NYC mics are cash only. Trying to perform without buying the drink at a bar mic is how rooms get cancelled.

## Frequently asked questions

### Is it rude to leave an open mic after your set?

Yes, and it is the most commonly cited breach of open mic etiquette. The audience at most mics is other comedians, so leaving early makes the room worse for the people after you. Stay for at least a few sets.

### What happens if you go over your time at an open mic?

The host will light you, meaning they signal that your time is nearly up. Ignoring it takes time from the comics after you and is the quickest way to stop getting spots at that room.

### Can you record your set at an open mic?

Usually yes, but ask the host first. Audio recording from a phone on a table is normally fine. Setting up cameras or tripods is not, and some rooms do not allow recording at all.

### What should you wear to an open mic?

Whatever you would wear to a bar. There is no dress code at NYC open mics, and dressing up marks you as new more than anything you say on stage.

### Should you tell the room it is your first open mic?

Opinions differ. It can buy goodwill from other comics who remember their own first night, but it can also read as asking for a pass. Most experienced comics advise just doing your jokes.

### Do you have to buy a drink at an open mic?

At mics with a one-drink or two-item minimum, yes. That is the arrangement that lets the venue host the room, and not honouring it is how mics lose their venues.

## Find a room

You can browse every [open mic running in New York](/open-mics) by night or by borough, with the cost, sign-up method and start time for each one.

Start with [Manhattan](/open-mics/manhattan), [Brooklyn](/open-mics/brooklyn) or [Queens](/open-mics/queens).
